claim: The nuclear genome of P. saccamoebae is 7.3 Mb in size on 221 scaffolds and possesses 3750 predicted genes.
source: Our approaches produced a target nuclear genome assembly of 7.3 Mb in size on 221 scaffolds and possesses 3750 predicted genes (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the genome assembly size, scaffold number, and gene count based on sequencing and assembly results.

claim: The genome size of P. saccamoebae is intermediate between R. allomycis (11.8 Mb) and M. daphniae (5.6 Mb).
source: This size is intermediate between R. allomycis (11.8 Mb) and M. daphniae (5.6 Mb), while the number of genes is similar to that of M. daphniae (3331 genes).
evidence: The comparison is made directly in the text and supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The GC content of P. saccamoebae is 47%, which is within the upper range of sequenced Rozellomycota and Microsporidia [34–47%].
source: The GC content is 47%, which is within the upper range of sequenced Rozellomycota and Microsporidia [34–47%] (Katinka et al., 2001; James et al., 2013).
evidence: The GC content is measured from the genome assembly and compared to published data from related organisms.

claim: Analysis of the core eukaryotic genes (CEGs) indicates that the P. saccamoebae assembly is fairly complete with identification of 89% of complete CEGs and 91% complete or partial CEGs.
source: Analysis of the core eukaryotic genes (CEGs) indicates that the assembly is fairly complete with identification of 89% of complete CEGs and 91% complete or partial CEGs.
evidence: CEGMA analysis was performed to assess assembly completeness, providing quantitative metrics.

claim: 50% of the P. saccamoebae genome resides on only 29 scaffolds.
source: As an additional measure of assembly continuity, we found that 50% of the genome resides on only 29 scaffolds.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the genome assembly (L50 statistic).

claim: Over 76% of the P. saccamoebae genome is covered by gene space.
source: Over 76% of the genome is covered by gene space, while repeated content covers only 0.53% of the genome, most of which are simple or low complexity repeats.
evidence: This is calculated from the genome annotation results.

claim: Repeated content covers only 0.53% of the P. saccamoebae genome, most of which are simple or low complexity repeats.
source: Over 76% of the genome is covered by gene space, while repeated content covers only 0.53% of the genome, most of which are simple or low complexity repeats.
evidence: This is determined from repeat analysis of the genome assembly.

claim: P. saccamoebae diverges within Rozellomycota after R. allomycis with strong support (MLBP = 100) but diverges before M. daphniae.
source: Within the clade, P. saccamoebae diverges within Rozellomycota after R. allomycis with strong support (MLBP = 100) but diverges before M. daphniae, which is still supported as the earliest diverging microsporidian species.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of 53 concatenated proteins with bootstrap support values, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Rozellomycota is reconstructed as paraphyletic with the current nomenclature.
source: With the current nomenclature, Rozellomycota is therefore reconstructed as paraphyletic.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic tree topology showing Microsporidia nested within Rozellomycota.

claim: Hypothesis testing of alternative placements of P. saccamoebae and Microsporidia were all rejected, supporting a paraphyletic Rozellomycota.
source: Hypothesis testing of alternative placements of P. saccamoebae and Microsporidia were all rejected, supporting a paraphyletic Rozellomycota (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and reanalysis of the data following removal of Microsporidia species (excluding M. daphniae) also gave support for a monophyletic Kingdom Fungi (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and for the branching order within Rozellomycota observed in analyses with Microsporidia included.
evidence: Statistical hypothesis testing (CONSEL) was performed on alternative tree topologies.

claim: P. saccamoebae shares the most of its 2470 orthogroups, 1975 (80%), with Spizellomyces punctatus.
source: We found P. saccamoebae shares the most of its 2470 orthogroups, 1975 (80%), with Spizellomyces punctatus (Figure 3B), a chytrid fungus which has been shown to share a few specific orthogroups with Microsporidia (Cuomo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on orthology clustering analysis comparing proteomes across multiple species.

claim: P. saccamoebae shares 1,722 (70%) orthogroups with R. allomycis and 1,357 (55%) with M. daphniae.
source: Although a substantial number of P. saccamoebae orthogroups are also shared with R. allomycis (1,722; 70%) and M. daphniae (1,357;55%), it shares more with many other distantly related Fungi, including species in the derived fungal phyla of Ascomycota and Basidiomycota, than with these two closer relatives.
evidence: This is determined from orthology clustering analysis.

claim: P. saccamoebae shares more orthogroups with many distantly related Fungi than with its two closer relatives R. allomycis and M. daphniae.
source: Although a substantial number of P. saccamoebae orthogroups are also shared with R. allomycis (1,722; 70%) and M. daphniae (1,357;55%), it shares more with many other distantly related Fungi, including species in the derived fungal phyla of Ascomycota and Basidiomycota, than with these two closer relatives.
evidence: This is inferred from comparative analysis of ortholog sharing patterns.

claim: The fewest P. saccamoebae orthogroups are shared with all other microsporidians sampled, 589 to 664 (24 to 27%).
source: The fewest P. saccamoebae orthogroups are shared with all other microsporidians sampled, 589 to 664 (24 to 27%).
evidence: This is determined from orthology clustering analysis.

claim: No orthogroups are universally present for Rozellomycota and microsporidians.
source: No orthogroups are universally present for Rozellomycota and microsporidians (Figure 3A), and very few clusters were specific to P. saccamoebae and either R. allomycis (12) or M. daphniae (13).
evidence: This is determined from orthology clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Very few orthogroup clusters were specific to P. saccamoebae and either R. allomycis (12) or M. daphniae (13).
source: No orthogroups are universally present for Rozellomycota and microsporidians (Figure 3A), and very few clusters were specific to P. saccamoebae and either R. allomycis (12) or M. daphniae (13).
evidence: This is determined from orthology clustering analysis.

claim: There are 377 orthogroups that P. saccamoebae shares with other Fungi that are not found in R. allomycis, M. daphniae, or Microsporidia.
source: There are 377 orthogroups that P. saccamoebae shares with other Fungi that are not found in R. allomycis, M. daphniae, or Microsporidia (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is determined from orthology clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Of the 377 orthogroups P. saccamoebae shares with other Fungi but not with R. allomycis, M. daphniae, or Microsporidia, eight are related to oxidative phosphorylation functions in the mitochondrion.
source: Of these, many have no hypothetical annotation, however, eight are related to oxidative phosphorylation functions in the mitochondrion, three are nuclear-pore-associated proteins, and two are proteins involved in converting ethanol to acetate (via alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases).
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of the orthogroups.

claim: Of the 377 orthogroups P. saccamoebae shares with other Fungi but not with R. allomycis, M. daphniae, or Microsporidia, three are nuclear-pore-associated proteins.
source: Of these, many have no hypothetical annotation, however, eight are related to oxidative phosphorylation functions in the mitochondrion, three are nuclear-pore-associated proteins, and two are proteins involved in converting ethanol to acetate (via alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases).
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of the orthogroups.

claim: Of the 377 orthogroups P. saccamoebae shares with other Fungi but not with R. allomycis, M. daphniae, or Microsporidia, two are proteins involved in converting ethanol to acetate (via alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases).
source: Of these, many have no hypothetical annotation, however, eight are related to oxidative phosphorylation functions in the mitochondrion, three are nuclear-pore-associated proteins, and two are proteins involved in converting ethanol to acetate (via alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases).
evidence: This is based on functional annotation of the orthogroups.

claim: Analysis of overall gene loss and gain revealed moderate loss leading to R. allomycis, followed by larger amounts of gene loss and lineage-specific gains in R. allomycis, P. saccamoebae, and M. daphniae.
source: Analysis of overall gene loss and gain revealed moderate loss leading to R. allomycis, followed by larger amounts of gene loss and lineage-specific gains in R. allomycis, P. saccamoebae, and M. daphniae (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on ancestral character state reconstruction of orthogroup presence/absence, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A circular mitochondrial genome of P. saccamoebae was assembled onto a single contig of 25,401 bp with 41 predicted genes.
source: A circular mitochondrial genome that contains a standard complement of fungal mitochondrial genes was assembled onto a single contig of 25,401 bp with 41 predicted genes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on genome assembly and annotation of the mitochondrial genome.

claim: The P. saccamoebae mitochondrial genome contains all genes typically found in fungal mitochondrial genomes that are involved in oxidative phosphorylation including those of Complex I (nad1, nad2, nad3, nad4, nad4L, nad5, and nad6).
source: All genes typically found in fungal mitochondrial genomes that are involved in oxidative phosphorylation are present including those of Complex I (nad1, nad2, nad3, nad4, nad4L, nad5, and nad6), Complex III (cob), Complex IV (cox1, cox2, and cox3), Complex V (atp6, atp8, and atp9), 23 tRNAs, one ribosomal protein (rps12), and the large and small rRNA subunits (rnL and rnS).
evidence: This is based on annotation of the mitochondrial genome.

claim: The P. saccamoebae mitochondrial genome contains genes for Complex III (cob), Complex IV (cox1, cox2, and cox3), and Complex V (atp6, atp8, and atp9).
source: All genes typically found in fungal mitochondrial genomes that are involved in oxidative phosphorylation are present including those of Complex I (nad1, nad2, nad3, nad4, nad4L, nad5, and nad6), Complex III (cob), Complex IV (cox1, cox2, and cox3), Complex V (atp6, atp8, and atp9), 23 tRNAs, one ribosomal protein (rps12), and the large and small rRNA subunits (rnL and rnS).
evidence: This is based on annotation of the mitochondrial genome.

claim: The P. saccamoebae mitochondrial genome contains 23 tRNAs, one ribosomal protein (rps12), and the large and small rRNA subunits (rnL and rnS).
source: All genes typically found in fungal mitochondrial genomes that are involved in oxidative phosphorylation are present including those of Complex I (nad1, nad2, nad3, nad4, nad4L, nad5, and nad6), Complex III (cob), Complex IV (cox1, cox2, and cox3), Complex V (atp6, atp8, and atp9), 23 tRNAs, one ribosomal protein (rps12), and the large and small rRNA subunits (rnL and rnS).
evidence: This is based on annotation of the mitochondrial genome.

claim: R. allomycis, M. daphniae, and the derived microsporidians have lost all Complex I genes or the entire mitochondrial genome altogether.
source: This is in contrast to R. allomycis, M. daphniae, and the derived microsporidians, which have, respectively, lost all Complex I genes or the entire mitochondrial genome altogether (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of mitochondrial genomes across species.

claim: P. saccamoebae possesses rps12, not rps3 like most fungal mitochondrial genomes.
source: Like R. allomycis and M. daphniae, P. saccamoebae possesses rps12, not rps3 like most fungal mitochondrial genomes (Aguileta et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2017), indicating these proteins have been differentially retained between these two lineages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on annotation of the mitochondrial genome and comparison with other fungi.

claim: Using conserved mitochondrial genes (cob, cox1, cox2, cox3, and atp6), P. saccamoebae mitochondrion is placed as sister to R. allomycis and M. daphniae, and not with the available amoebozoan mitochondrial sequences.
source: Using the conserved mitochondrial genes (cob, cox1, cox2, cox3, and atp6), P. saccamoebae mitochondrion is placed as sister to R. allomycis and M. daphniae, and not with the available amoebozoan mitochondrial sequences (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis of mitochondrial genes.

claim: Supplementary genes involved in the electron transport chain (including ferrodoxin, ubiquinone, succinate dehydrogenase, etc.) are present in the nuclear genome of P. saccamoebae, in addition to being expressed.
source: Moreover, supplementary genes involved in the electron transport chain (including ferrodoxin, ubiquinone, succinate dehydrogenase, etc.) are present in the nuclear genome of P. saccamoebae, in addition to being expressed, suggesting it possesses full oxidative phosphorylation functionality.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and RNA-seq data.

claim: P. saccamoebae possesses full oxidative phosphorylation functionality.
source: Moreover, supplementary genes involved in the electron transport chain (including ferrodoxin, ubiquinone, succinate dehydrogenase, etc.) are present in the nuclear genome of P. saccamoebae, in addition to being expressed, suggesting it possesses full oxidative phosphorylation functionality.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence and expression of all necessary genes for oxidative phosphorylation.

claim: The genes necessary for de novo nucleotide (both purine and pyrimidine) biosynthesis are all absent in P. saccamoebae.
source: The genes necessary for de novo nucleotide (both purine and pyrimidine) biosynthesis are all absent in P. saccamoebae, suggesting it is not capable of producing its own nucleotides, and it also lacks genes for converting nucleosides to nucleotides and vice versa (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and pathway analysis.

claim: P. saccamoebae is not capable of producing its own nucleotides.
source: The genes necessary for de novo nucleotide (both purine and pyrimidine) biosynthesis are all absent in P. saccamoebae, suggesting it is not capable of producing its own nucleotides, and it also lacks genes for converting nucleosides to nucleotides and vice versa (Figure 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of nucleotide biosynthesis genes.

claim: P. saccamoebae lacks genes for converting nucleosides to nucleotides and vice versa.
source: The genes necessary for de novo nucleotide (both purine and pyrimidine) biosynthesis are all absent in P. saccamoebae, suggesting it is not capable of producing its own nucleotides, and it also lacks genes for converting nucleosides to nucleotides and vice versa (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and pathway analysis.

claim: One of the most highly expressed transporter genes in P. saccamoebae is a nucleoside transporter (PSACC_00918), which has homologs in many other Fungi including M. daphniae, but which is not found in R. allomycis.
source: One of the most highly expressed transporter genes is a nucleoside transporter (PSACC_00918), which has homologs in many other Fungi including M. daphniae, but which is not found in R. allomycis.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data and comparative genomics.

claim: Another nucleoside transporter (PSACC_02618) was identified in P. saccamoebae and is expressed.
source: Another nucleoside transporter (PSACC_02618) was also identified and is expressed.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and RNA-seq data.

claim: Other highly expressed transporters in P. saccamoebae include an ABC transporter (PSACC_00512), an Na+ dicarboxylate and phosphate transporter (PSACC_03652) and a general substrate transporter (PSACC_01530).
source: Other highly expressed transporters include an ABC transporter (PSACC_00512), an Na+ dicarboxylate and phosphate transporter (PSACC_03652) and a general substrate transporter (PSACC_01530).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq expression data.

claim: There is no evidence for the presence of the horizontally acquired thymidine kinases found by Alexander et al. (2016) in both R. allomycis and several microsporidians in P. saccamoebae.
source: There is no evidence for the presence of the horizontally acquired thymidine kinases found by Alexander et al. (2016) in both R. allomycis and several microsporidians.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and comparison with published findings.

claim: Many amino acid biosynthesis pathways are reduced or absent in P. saccamoebae.
source: Many amino acid biosynthesis pathways are reduced or absent in P. saccamoebae (Figure 6A), and as a result it is likely that it does not produce histidine or tryptophan, and may require intermediates from the host to complete synthesis of the following: lysine, methionine, arginine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, leucine, valine, and proline.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and pathway analysis.

claim: P. saccamoebae likely does not produce histidine or tryptophan.
source: Many amino acid biosynthesis pathways are reduced or absent in P. saccamoebae (Figure 6A), and as a result it is likely that it does not produce histidine or tryptophan, and may require intermediates from the host to complete synthesis of the following: lysine, methionine, arginine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, leucine, valine, and proline.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of biosynthesis pathway genes.

claim: P. saccamoebae may require intermediates from the host to complete synthesis of lysine, methionine, arginine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, leucine, valine, and proline.
source: Many amino acid biosynthesis pathways are reduced or absent in P. saccamoebae (Figure 6A), and as a result it is likely that it does not produce histidine or tryptophan, and may require intermediates from the host to complete synthesis of the following: lysine, methionine, arginine, phenylalanine, isoleucine, leucine, valine, and proline.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete biosynthesis pathways.

claim: For synthesis of branched chain amino acids (valine, leucine, and isoleucine), a single protein, a homolog of branched chain amino acid aminotransferase (PSACC_01141 in P. saccamoebae), is present and expressed based on mRNA-seq data.
source: For synthesis of branched chain amino acids (valine, leucine, and isoleucine), a single protein, a homolog of branched chain amino acid aminotransferase (PSACC_01141 in P. saccamoebae), is present and expressed based on our mRNA-seq data.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and RNA-seq data.

claim: R. allomycis and M. daphniae have similar yet unique profiles of reductions in amino acid biosynthesis enzymes.
source: Our investigations also revealed similar yet unique profiles of reductions in amino acid biosynthesis enzymes in R. allomycis and M. daphniae as well (Figure 6A), while the rest of Microsporidia cannot produce any amino acids.
evidence: This is based on comparative genome analysis.

claim: The rest of Microsporidia cannot produce any amino acids.
source: Our investigations also revealed similar yet unique profiles of reductions in amino acid biosynthesis enzymes in R. allomycis and M. daphniae as well (Figure 6A), while the rest of Microsporidia cannot produce any amino acids.
evidence: This is based on comparative genome analysis.

claim: Two expressed amino acid permeases (PSACC_02864 and PSACC_03255) were identified in P. saccamoebae that are homologous to a single permease in both R. allomycis and M. daphniae and most closely related to bacterial, not fungal, amino acid permeases.
source: We identified two expressed amino acid permeases (PSACC_02864 and PSACC_03255) that may offset these gene losses in the P. saccamoebae genome, which are homologous to a single permease in both R. allomycis and M. daphniae and most closely related to bacterial, not fungal, amino acid permeases (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation, RNA-seq data, and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: There are three fungal chitin synthase domain containing proteins in P. saccamoebae (PSACC_00558, PSACC_00865, PSACC_01336).
source: There are three fungal chitin synthase domain containing proteins in P. saccamoebae (PSACC_00558, PSACC_00865, PSACC_01336).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation.

claim: All three chitin synthases in P. saccamoebae are Division I chitin synthases with homologs in R. allomycis.
source: These are all Division I chitin synthases with homologs in R. allomycis.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and comparison.

claim: Unlike R. allomycis, no Division II chitin synthases were identified in P. saccamoebae, a characteristic P. saccamoebae shares with Microsporidia.
source: Unlike R. allomycis, no Division II chitin synthases were identified, a characteristic P. saccamoebae shares with Microsporidia.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and comparative analysis.

claim: P. saccamoebae has almost all of the conventional meiosis-related genes, including all known meiosis-specific genes (Rec8, Spo11-1, Dmc1, Hop2, Mnd1, Msh4, and Msh5).
source: P. saccamoebae has almost all of the conventional meiosis-related genes, including all known meiosis-specific genes (Rec8, Spo11-1, Dmc1, Hop2, Mnd1, Msh4, and Msh5; Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and comparison with known meiosis genes.

claim: The only meiosis-related gene absent from the P. saccamoebae genome is a homolog of Mlh3 which is involved in DNA mismatch repair and appears to be absent in all other members of this earliest diverging fungal clade.
source: The only meiosis-related gene absent from the P. saccamoebae genome is a homolog of Mlh3 which is involved in DNA mismatch repair and appears to be absent in all other members of this earliest diverging fungal clade.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and comparative analysis.

claim: The number of meiosis genes found in P. saccamoebae is greater than any other sequenced Rozellomycota or Microsporidia with available genomes.
source: The number of meiosis genes found in P. saccamoebae is greater than any other sequenced Rozellomycota or Microsporidia with available genomes.
evidence: This is based on comparative genome analysis.

claim: P. saccamoebae is theoretically able to undergo conventional meiotic recombination.
source: This indicates that this obligate intracellular parasite is theoretically able to undergo conventional meiotic recombination, which is bolstered by analysis of SNP frequencies that revealed that the vast majority of alleles possess a 50:50 ratio, indicating that P. saccamoebae is likely diploid, like most microsporidian species examined to date (Figure 7B) (Cuomo et al., 2012; Haag et al., 2013a, 2013b; Selman et al., 2013; Ndikumana et al., 2017; Pelin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of meiosis genes and SNP analysis.

claim: Analysis of SNP frequencies revealed that the vast majority of alleles in P. saccamoebae possess a 50:50 ratio, indicating that P. saccamoebae is likely diploid.
source: This indicates that this obligate intracellular parasite is theoretically able to undergo conventional meiotic recombination, which is bolstered by analysis of SNP frequencies that revealed that the vast majority of alleles possess a 50:50 ratio, indicating that P. saccamoebae is likely diploid, like most microsporidian species examined to date (Figure 7B) (Cuomo et al., 2012; Haag et al., 2013a, 2013b; Selman et al., 2013; Ndikumana et al., 2017; Pelin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on SNP frequency analysis from genomic data.

claim: P. saccamoebae is likely diploid, like most microsporidian species examined to date.
source: This indicates that this obligate intracellular parasite is theoretically able to undergo conventional meiotic recombination, which is bolstered by analysis of SNP frequencies that revealed that the vast majority of alleles possess a 50:50 ratio, indicating that P. saccamoebae is likely diploid, like most microsporidian species examined to date (Figure 7B) (Cuomo et al., 2012; Haag et al., 2013a, 2013b; Selman et al., 2013; Ndikumana et al., 2017; Pelin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from SNP analysis and comparison with published data on microsporidians.

claim: P. saccamoebae has two putative homeodomains (HD1 and HD2 homologs) (PSACC_01945 and PSACC_01946) whose genome organization is strikingly similar to that found in loci that govern sexual identity in more derived Fungi, particularly Basidiomycota.
source: Other P. saccamoebae genes potentially involved in mating include two putative homeodomains (HD1 and HD2 homologs) (PSACC_01945 and PSACC_01946) whose genome organization is strikingly similar to that found in loci that govern sexual identity in more derived Fungi, particularly Basidiomycota.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and comparative analysis.

claim: Heterozygosity and extensive allelic divergence typical of fungal MAT-loci is absent along the P. saccamoebae homeodomain genes.
source: However, heterozygosity and extensive allelic divergence typical of fungal MAT-loci is absent along those genes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the genomic region containing the homeodomain genes.

claim: The genome organization of the homeodomain genes is not found to be conserved in other Rozellomycota and Microsporidia.
source: Furthermore, their genome organization is not found to be conserved in other Rozellomycota and Microsporidia.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Divergent copies of both HD1 and HD2 exist at other locations in the genome of the microsporidians Pseudoloma neurophilia and Nosema ceranae.
source: Intriguingly, divergent copies of both HD1 and HD2 exist at other locations in the genome of the microsporidians Pseudoloma neurophilia and Nosema ceranae (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), but none of these show the organization or divergence expected for fungal-like MAT loci.
evidence: This is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: Unlike Rozella spp. and environmentally acquired Rozellomycota targeted using FISH, P. saccamoebae does not possess the ability to produce a flagellum.
source: This revealed that unlike Rozella spp. and environmentally acquired Rozellomycota targeted using FISH (Jones et al., 2011), P. saccamoebae does not possess the ability to produce a flagellum (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation searching for flagellum-related genes.

claim: Using hidden Markov models (HMMs) developed using alignments of known polar filament proteins (PFPs) in Microsporidia, no significant hits were found in the predicted proteome of P. saccamoebae (all conditional p>0.001).
source: Using hidden Markov models (HMMs) developed using alignments of known polar filament proteins (PFPs) in Microsporidia (Han and Weiss, 2017), we searched the predicted proteome of P. saccamoebae for sequence-based evidence of PFPs and found no significant hits (all conditional p>0.001).
evidence: This is based on HMM searches of the proteome.

claim: The failure to detect PFPs in P. saccamoebae likely reflects the rapid rate of evolution of these proteins, which are only known from species with a well-developed polar filament.
source: This likely reflects the rapid rate of evolution of these proteins, which are only known from species with a well-developed polar filament.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the negative search results.

claim: The HMMs for polar filament proteins similarly did not detect PFPs from M. daphniae, but detected all PFPs in the microsporidian Encephalitozoon romaleae.
source: Our HMMs similarly did not detect PFPs from M. daphniae, but detected all PFPs in the microsporidian Encephalitozoon romaleae.
evidence: This is based on HMM searches as a control experiment.

claim: The existence of a typical fungal mitochondrial genome, with a complete electron transport chain in P. saccamoebae is in stark contrast with the hypothesis of gradual reduction of oxidative respiration function within the Rozellomycota-Microsporidia clade eventually leading to the origin of mitosomes in Microsporidia.
source: The existence of a typical fungal mitochondrial genome, with a complete electron transport chain in P. saccamoebae is in stark contrast with the hypothesis of gradual reduction of oxidative respiration function within the Rozellomycota-Microsporidia clade eventually leading to the origin of mitosomes in Microsporidia (Tsaousis et al., 2008; James et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mitochondrial genome data contradicting a previous hypothesis.

claim: A mitochondrion was not identified using electron microscopy in the original species description of P. saccamoebae.
source: Similar to what was found in M. daphniae, a mitochondrion was not identified using electron microscopy in the original species description of P. saccamoebae (Corsaro et al., 2014), indicating that organelles can be difficult to discern in micrographs of these very small (~1 µm) endoparasites.
evidence: This is based on published microscopy observations.

claim: Organelles can be difficult to discern in micrographs of very small (~1 µm) endoparasites.
source: Similar to what was found in M. daphniae, a mitochondrion was not identified using electron microscopy in the original species description of P. saccamoebae (Corsaro et al., 2014), indicating that organelles can be difficult to discern in micrographs of these very small (~1 µm) endoparasites.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between microscopy and genomic evidence.

claim: In both M. daphniae and P. saccamoebae, the only evidence for a functional mitochondrion lies in the genomic data.
source: In fact, in both M. daphniae (Haag et al., 2014), and P. saccamoebae, the only evidence for a functional mitochondrion lies in the genomic data, yet interpretation of this data should be considered indisputable.
evidence: This is based on comparison of microscopy and genomic data.

claim: The presence of all genes in Complex I of oxidative phosphorylation in P. saccamoebae, taken in concert with the phylogenetic results, indicates that the reductions in R. allomycis and M. daphniae mitochondrial genomes represent independent and convergent losses.
source: However, the presence of all genes in Complex I of oxidative phosphorylation in P. saccamoebae, taken in concert with the phylogenetic results, indicates that the reductions in R. allomycis and M. daphniae mitochondrial genomes represent independent and convergent losses.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic position of P. saccamoebae and the presence of Complex I genes.

claim: The independent reductions in Complex I suggests that there may have been multiple transitions to intracellular parasitism.
source: The independent reductions in Complex I suggests that there may have been multiple transitions to intracellular parasitism and that putative 'epiphytic' Rozellomycota are or were once occupying non-parasitic ecological niches (Jones et al., 2011; Ishida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the pattern of gene loss.

claim: One explanation for the maintenance of a fully functioning mitochondrion in P. saccamoebae could be related to its subcellular location.
source: One explanation for the maintenance of a fully functioning mitochondrion in P. saccamoebae could be related to its subcellular location.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the biological significance of the findings.

claim: Studies using light microscopy of R. allomycis and Microsporidia have found that these parasites are surrounded by host mitochondria, presumably to facilitate energy theft from the host.

source: The loss of biosynthesis of nucleotides and multiple amino acids in P. saccamoebae indicates that like R. allomycis and Microsporidia (Dean et al., 2016), this species is highly dependent on its host for aspects of both protein synthesis and DNA replication.

source: P. saccamoebae also lacks a homolog of the nucleotide transporters (identified in R. allomycis and Microsporidia) which were horizontally acquired from Chlamydiae (Tsaousis et al., 2008), but M. daphniae lacks these as well (Haag et al., 2014) suggesting these have either been missed in the genome assemblies, that this acquisition happened at least two independent times, or that the gene has been independently lost in both P. saccamoebae and M. daphniae after horizontal transfer into the ancestor of Rozellomycota.
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and comparison with published data.
